seo.description: Chapter six of the uv course. uv init, pyproject.toml read line by line, requires-python as a promise, --app vs --lib vs --package vs --bare, what changed in uv 0.12, and why .venv and uv.lock appear without being asked for.

scenes.narration: One word makes a project. But what did those six files actually do?

data.headline: SIX FILES, ONE WORD
data.subtext: and every one has a job

scenes.narration: One command — uv init, and a project name — and a project exists. Six things appeared, none of which you typed. Most tutorials skip straight past this and start installing packages. We're going to read every single file instead, because a project you can't read is a project you can't fix.

uvStage.headline: Six things, from [one] word
uvStage.premise: One command wrote all of these. Nothing here is decoration.

steps.label: uv init hello-world && ls -a hello-world
steps.detail: six things, and you typed none of them

stage.label: pyproject.toml
stage.sub: what your project is, and needs

stage.label: .gitignore
stage.sub: written for you, and it excludes .venv

scenes.narration: Welcome back. This chapter builds a real project and reads every line of it, so nothing in your own folder is ever a mystery again.

data.title: Your first real project
data.subtitle: uv, chapter six · every file, line by line

scenes.narration: Start with the file everything else hangs off.

pyproject dot toml is the standard way a Python project describes itself, which is why every modern tool reads it and none of them need convincing. Not a uv invention, in other words — a Python standard that uv happens to follow properly. Four sections, and we'll take them one at a time.

uvStage.headline: The file everything [reads]
uvStage.premise: A Python standard, not a uv invention. Every modern tool understands it.

steps.label: cat pyproject.toml
steps.detail: four sections, and nothing else

steps.label: grep -c . pyproject.toml
steps.detail: eighteen lines is the whole description

steps.label: uv run python -c "import tomllib; print(1)"
steps.detail: and Python itself can read this format

scenes.narration: Name and version identify the project. Description and readme are for humans. Authors is written from your local git configuration, so check what landed there before you publish anything — that line goes out into the world with your package.

uvStage.headline: Check the [authors] line
uvStage.premise: uv reads your local git config to fill this in. Read it before publishing.

steps.label: grep -A2 authors pyproject.toml
steps.detail: yours came from git config, not from uv

stage.label: name
stage.sub: what the package will be called

stage.label: authors
stage.sub: read this one before you publish

scenes.narration: Requires-python is a promise, not a preference. It says which interpreters your code claims to work on, and uv refuses to add any package that can't satisfy it. So this one line quietly shapes every dependency decision that follows.

uvStage.headline: requires-python is a [promise]
uvStage.premise: A claim about what your code supports. uv enforces it on every package you add.

steps.label: uv add "some-3-13-only-package"
out: x No solution found when resolving dependencies:
Because your project requires-python is >=3.10 and
steps.detail: the promise refused the package

scenes.narration: Dependencies starts as an empty list, and next chapter fills it. Then build-system, which tells anyone packaging your code which machinery to use. Notice the constraint written there is less than nought point thirteen point zero, even though the documentation page shows it without the trailing zero. Trust the file.

uvStage.headline: Trust the [file], not the page
uvStage.premise: The docs render the constraint one way. The file on disk writes it another.

steps.label: grep -A2 build-system pyproject.toml
steps.detail: the docs show <0.13. the file writes <0.13.0.

steps.label: grep dependencies pyproject.toml
steps.detail: empty, for exactly one more chapter

steps.label: uv build 2>&1 | head -2
steps.detail: and that build-system is what makes this work

scenes.narration: Now, a warning about every older tutorial you're going to find.

The documentation says it plainly: prior to version nought point twelve, uv did not define a build system for applications by default. Which means a tutorial recorded last year shows a different set of files from the ones you just got. Nothing is broken — the tool moved.

uvStage.headline: Older tutorials look [different]
uvStage.premise: uv 0.12 changed what init writes. A mismatch means the video is old, not you.

steps.label: uv --version
steps.detail: check this before trusting any tutorial

stage.label: pyproject.toml
stage.sub: and this is why your file differs

scenes.narration: There are four shapes uv can make, and the flag you pass decides which. App is the default, meaning something you run. Lib is something other people import, so uv puts your code under a src folder to keep the import path honest. Packaged gives you a command name. And bare writes almost nothing, because sometimes you'd rather decide everything yourself.

uvStage.headline: Four shapes, [one] command
uvStage.premise: The flag decides the tree. Pick by what the thing is, not by what looks tidy.

steps.label: uv init --lib mylib && ls mylib/src/mylib
steps.detail: a library puts your code under src

stage.label: --package
stage.sub: installs a name you can type

stage.label: --bare
stage.sub: when you want to decide yourself

scenes.narration: And the rest of the files, quickly, because none of them hide anything.

chapter.title: The other files
chapter.subtitle: and the ones that appear later

scenes.narration: Dot python dash version is the pin from last chapter, written from whatever interpreter uv chose. Main dot py is a one-line starter file, so the project runs the moment it exists. README is empty and yours to fill in. And dot gitignore already excludes dot venv, which means you cannot accidentally commit an entire environment to your repository.

uvStage.headline: Nothing here is [hidden]
uvStage.premise: Four small files, each doing one obvious job, all of them readable.

steps.label: cat .python-version .gitignore
steps.detail: uv excluded .venv without being asked

stage.label: main.py
stage.sub: a hello world, so it runs immediately

stage.label: README.md
stage.sub: empty, and yours to fill in

stage.label: .gitignore
stage.sub: so you cannot commit an environment

scenes.narration: Two more files turn up later without being asked for. Dot venv is the project's own shelf, and uv lock is the exact list of what's on it. Neither is something you create; both appear the first time you add a dependency or run anything.

uvStage.headline: Two more [arrive] later
uvStage.premise: Nobody creates these. They appear the first time uv has to build anything.

steps.label: uv run main.py
steps.detail: the shelf was built on the way past

stage.label: uv.lock
stage.sub: exactly what is on that shelf

scenes.narration: One command deserves special attention, and you'll type it constantly. uv run does the whole ritual from chapter zero on your behalf: check the environment exists, make it if not, make sure the packages match, then run your code inside it. Four steps, invisible, every time.

uvStage.headline: uv run does [all four]
uvStage.premise: The ritual from chapter zero, performed for you, before every single command.

steps.label: uv run main.py
steps.detail: made, checked, used — in one line

stage.label: uv run main.py
stage.sub: and you never think about any of it

scenes.narration: If you asked for a packaged project, one more section appears. Project scripts maps a command name to a function in your code, and after that uv run followed by that name runs your function directly. Which is how a Python project turns into something with an actual command.

uvStage.headline: Give it a [command] name
uvStage.premise: [project.scripts] maps a name you can type to a function in your code.

steps.label: grep -A2 "project.scripts" pyproject.toml
steps.detail: a name, and the function behind it

steps.label: uv run hello-world
steps.detail: and now the name itself is runnable

steps.label: uv run python -c "import hello_world"
steps.detail: importable too, because it is packaged

scenes.narration: It's worth knowing that uv init will happily take over a folder you already have. Point it at a directory with code in it and uv writes only what's missing, which means adopting an existing project is one command rather than an afternoon of copying files around.

uvStage.headline: It [adopts] existing folders
uvStage.premise: uv init in a folder that already has code writes only the pieces missing.

steps.label: ls
steps.detail: three years of files, and no project

steps.label: uv init --bare --name old-scripts .
steps.detail: and nothing of yours was overwritten

scenes.narration: One more thing worth doing on day one. uv init made a git repository for you, and now is the moment to decide what belongs in it. The project file, the pin and the lockfile all go in. The environment folder does not, because uv already excluded it on your behalf.

uvStage.headline: What goes in [git]
uvStage.premise: Everything that describes the project is committed. The built shelf never is.

steps.label: git status --short
steps.detail: notice .venv is not even offered

stage.label: uv.lock
stage.sub: so colleagues get your exact packages

scenes.narration: And if you'd rather not have a git repository at all, dash dash no dash vcs skips it. Small thing, but worth knowing before uv creates a repository inside a repository and your version control starts behaving strangely.

uvStage.headline: Skip the repo with [--no-vcs]
uvStage.premise: uv init makes a git repo by default. Inside another repo, that is rarely wanted.

steps.label: uv init packages/parser
steps.detail: a git repo, inside your git repo

steps.label: uv init --no-vcs packages/parser
steps.detail: better, inside a repository you already have

scenes.narration: Quick check. You just ran uv init and there's no dot venv folder anywhere. Did something go wrong? Pause the video here and decide for yourself before I answer. Ready? No — the environment appears the first time uv actually needs one.

quiz.question: uv init finished and there is no .venv. Is that a problem?
quiz.why: uv builds it the first time it has something to put in it.

scenes.narration: So, to recap. pyproject dot toml describes your project and every modern tool reads it. Requires-python is a promise that constrains every package you'll ever add. And the environment and the lockfile arrive by themselves, the first time uv needs them.

points.text: pyproject.toml is a standard, not a uv file
